approach: Work in the lift's frame: its upward retardation adds a downward pseudo force, so the body slides down with effective gravity g + a instead of g.

steps.text: The lift moves down but is slowing down, so its acceleration points upward, with size a. In the lift's frame, this adds a pseudo force on the body, directed downward.
The effective downward pull on the body is now gravity plus the pseudo force, so the effective gravity is g + a.
The incline is smooth, so the only force along the incline is the component of the effective weight along it. Find the acceleration down the incline.
Use the equation for distance from rest to find the time to slide the full length L.
steps.equation: L = ½(g + a)sinθ · t² ⇒ t = √(2L / ((g + a) sinθ))

common_mistakes.text: Treating the lift's retardation as making the effective gravity smaller instead of larger gives g − a in place of g + a.
Ignoring the lift's motion entirely and using plain gravity gives the answer for a stationary lift, √(2L / (g sinθ)).
